$comment: Events in 2026 that changed where Flock cameras operate, who pays for them or how their data is kept, as reported in the sources on this site. Kinds: added (new, renewed or kept contracts), ended (cameras switched off or removed), restricted (a law or order limiting use, funding or placement), flock (the company's own changes). Dates are those the sources give; precision says whether the day is known.
rule: Selection: decisions in 2026 by a state, a city or county, or Flock, as reported in the sources on this site, chosen to include contracts added and kept as well as cameras switched off. Not a complete list.

events.text: A new law requires deletion after 21 days unless the data is needed as evidence, limits use to felonies and gross misdemeanors, vehicles that are stolen or registered to people with arrest warrants, and missing or endangered people, and bars most sharing.
The council votes 5 to 4 to keep the town’s cameras, off since February, switched off.
The council extends the city’s contract for six months, with no sharing with outside agencies and a public transparency portal.
The council votes 6 to 4 for a five-year, $2.1 million contract.
WJAR reports that the State Police will install 39 plate readers statewide under a $597,000 Flock contract signed months earlier.
Makes seven days the default for keeping reads for new customers, down from 30; existing customers keep their settings.
The council votes 5 to 3 to renew the city’s Flock contract, worth about $270,000.
The governor orders state agencies to pause funding for Flock cameras; a state grant program had helped install at least 3,200.
The transportation department revokes permits for cameras on state road rights of way.
Police say they will switch off 321 of the department’s 684 cameras, those paid for with state grants.
The Department of Public Safety says it will pause installing more cameras but keep using its own, at least 940 according to an email a lawmaker shared.
After a meeting with Flock’s chief executive, police say the grant-funded cameras will stay on for at least 90 days; The Texas Tribune reports that Flock paused the city’s payments for them.
